clue.text: Fires cheerleaders for warning sailors

definitions.note: a noun phrase: things that warn sailors

blocks.note: fires and lights both mean flames or lamps that burn
a cheer is led off with 'hip, hip', so the leaders of a cheer are these

explanation.surface: Someone sacks the cheerleaders for heckling or alerting a crew of sailors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheerleaders' are not pom-pom girls: they are the words that lead off a cheer, as in 'hip, hip, hooray'.
explanation.definitionFit: Lightships are moored vessels carrying beacons that alert passing shipping to hazards such as sandbanks.

clue.text: Protestant who went too far for Danish queen

definitions.text: Protestant who went too far for Danish queen

blocks.note: surface reading: a religious zealot, a Protestant extremist
setter's reading: in Hamlet, Queen Gertrude of Denmark says of the Player Queen that she doth protest too much, methinks

explanation.walkthrough: 'Protestant' is not a churchgoer but one who protests, and Gertrude judges that the woman in the play-within-the-play protests too much.
explanation.definitionFit: Gertrude's famous line names the woman on stage, 'The ___ doth protest too much', so she is the protester who overdid it.

clue.text: Call to be silent produces surprised expression

blocks.note: to go is to make a call or sound, as in 'the cow goes moo'
the hushing sound telling someone to be quiet

explanation.surface: Telling someone to hush makes them look startled.
explanation.definitionFit: Gosh is a mild exclamation of astonishment, a minced form of an oath, so it is something said in surprise.

clue.text: Normally seeing score repeated

definitions.note: an adjective phrase: with normal sight

blocks.note: a score is twenty
the same number said a second time

explanation.surface: A sighted spectator sees the same scoreline come up again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Score' is not a match result but the number twenty, written twice.
explanation.definitionFit: Twenty-twenty vision is the standard measure of normal eyesight in an optician's chart test.

clue.text: Almost cause commander's ruin

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is lost

blocks.note: to have something done is to cause it to be done
OC is the abbreviation for Officer Commanding

explanation.surface: A commander nearly brings about his own downfall.
explanation.definitionFit: Havoc means widespread destruction and devastation, so it matches ruin as a noun.

clue.text: The Elephant's child was a tidy one

definitions.text: The Elephant's child was a tidy one

blocks.note: surface reading: the hero of Kipling's Just So story, who got his trunk from a crocodile
setter's reading: a tidy one is a sizeable one, so the child was a fair-sized thick-skinned beast

explanation.walkthrough: 'Tidy' suggests neatness, but here it means considerable, as in a tidy sum.
explanation.definitionFit: Pachyderm is the old zoological name for thick-skinned mammals such as elephants, so the young elephant was one.

clue.text: One bird's beginning is this one's completion

definitions.text: One bird's beginning is this one's completion

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
the opening letter of bird
taken as written

explanation.surface: A riddle about where one bird starts and another finishes.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does both jobs: one, a bird's first letter and 'is' together complete the bird the clue is talking about.
explanation.definitionFit: The ibis is a long-legged wading bird with a curved bill, sacred in ancient Egypt, so the clue describes a bird.

clue.text: Interrupting criminal activity

blocks.note: first meaning: cutting into a conversation
second meaning: forcing entry to a building to burgle it

explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both butting into someone's talk and burglars forcing their way into a house.

clue.text: Eyes tourists

blocks.note: first meaning, read cryptically: eyes are what see the sights
second meaning: visitors touring famous places

explanation.walkthrough: 'Eyes' looks like a verb, as in 'eyes up the tourists', but it is a plural noun taken whimsically.
explanation.definitionFit: Visitors who go round famous landmarks are called this, and eyes literally behold views.

clue.text: Girl's opening shot is wrong

definitions.note: a noun here: a wrong done to someone

blocks.note: Di is a short girl's name, with the 's
in tennis the opening shot of each point is the serve, or service

explanation.surface: A girl's first serve in a tennis match goes astray.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrong' looks like an adjective describing the shot, but it is a noun, an injury done to someone.
explanation.definitionFit: A disservice is a harmful action or injury done to someone, which is what a wrong means as a noun.

clue.text: Modern composer could be really cool), in the main

definitions.text: could be really cool), in the main

blocks.note: first meaning: Alban ..., the twentieth-century Austrian composer of Wozzeck

blocks.clueFragment: could be really cool), in the main
blocks.note: second meaning: an iceberg floating in the sea, which is cold indeed

explanation.walkthrough: 'The main' is an old word for the open sea, and a berg is short for iceberg.
explanation.definitionFit: Alban Berg was a modernist composer, and an iceberg is a mass of ice drifting in the ocean.

clue.text: Wife had £5 arranged for this tenancy

definitions.note: a place: the house in Anne Brontë's The Tenant of ___

indicators.note: arranged means set out in order, so the letters are put into a fresh sequence

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
the pound sign stands for L, from Latin libra, and five of them are wanted

explanation.surface: A wife pays a few pounds to arrange her lease.
explanation.walkthrough: '£5' reads as a sum of money, but it is five pound signs, five Ls. 'Tenancy' points to Anne Brontë's novel The Tenant of Wildfell Hall.
explanation.definitionFit: Helen Graham is the mysterious tenant of the old house in Anne Brontë's novel, so it is the place she rents.

clue.text: Newly painted gate creates awkward situation

blocks.note: first meaning, taken literally: a small gate with wet paint still tacky on it
second meaning: the idiom for a difficult position, from a damp cricket pitch

explanation.surface: Wet paint on a gate leaves someone in an awkward spot.
explanation.walkthrough: A wicket is a small gate; in cricket, a sticky wicket is a drying pitch on which the ball behaves unpredictably, hence the idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a tricky or difficult predicament, from the cricket pitch that makes batting hard.

clue.text: One could make Eastern rats panic

definitions.text: One could make Eastern rats panic

indicators.note: panic throws things into disorder, so the letters scatter into a new arrangement

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for Eastern
taken as written
the indicator word also supplies letters, taken as written

explanation.surface: A creature from the East could send rodents into a frenzy.
explanation.walkthrough: Shuffle E, RATS and PANIC; the whole clue is also the definition, since a cat from Persia, in the East, frightens rats.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-haired breed of domestic feline from Iran, and any feline scares rodents.

clue.text: Excellent police officer meets' con man

blocks.note: short for superintendent, a senior police rank
a con man dupes, or tricks, his victims

explanation.surface: A senior policeman comes face to face with a fraudster.
explanation.definitionFit: Super-duper is jokey slang for marvellous or first-rate, an informal term of high praise.

clue.text: Even includes it for fair result

indicators.note: a word that includes something holds it inside itself

blocks.note: equable means even, steady, not easily disturbed
taken as written

explanation.surface: An even split that includes everything gives a fair outcome.
explanation.definitionFit: Equitable means just and impartial, treating everyone alike, so it matches fair.

clue.text: One of James's people who harboured tea?

blocks.note: first meaning: a character in Henry James's novel The ...
second meaning, cryptic: in 1773 colonists tipped British tea into their city's harbour, the Tea Party

explanation.walkthrough: 'James' is the novelist Henry James, not a king; the question mark flags the jokey sense of harboured.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of the Massachusetts capital, the city of the Tea Party protest and the title of a Henry James novel.

clue.text: Poet accepted in society, we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is a sound, so the spelling is set aside

blocks.note: the done thing is what polite society accepts

explanation.surface: A poet is taken up by fashionable society, so people say.
explanation.walkthrough: John Donne's name is pronounced 'dun', just like done.
explanation.definitionFit: John Donne was the seventeenth-century English metaphysical writer of sonnets and sermons.

clue.text: Once perilous, perhaps, this investment

blocks.note: first meaning: an old word for a seat
second meaning: to invest a town is to surround it with troops

explanation.surface: An investment that was once risky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Investment' looks financial, but in military language it means besieging a place. The Siege Perilous was the seat at the Round Table reserved for the knight who would find the Grail.
explanation.definitionFit: The word once meant a seat or throne, and still means the surrounding and blockade of a fortified town.

clue.text: Butler translated Moliere manuscript

indicators.note: translated means turned into another form, so the letters are converted into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
MS is the standard abbreviation for manuscript

explanation.surface: A man named Butler renders a Molière manuscript into English.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Butler' looks like a translator's surname; it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A sommelier is the wine waiter of a restaurant, the modern equivalent of a butler in charge of the wine cellar.

clue.text: Summer's activity friend joins in as well

blocks.note: a summer is someone who sums, and summing is this
an ally is a friend

explanation.surface: A friend joins in with the holiday fun of summertime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Summer' is not the season but one who does sums.
explanation.definitionFit: Additionally is an adverb meaning also, besides or too, just like the phrase used.

clue.text: Quick breathing

blocks.note: first meaning: the old sense of living, as in the quick and the dead
second meaning: still drawing breath

explanation.walkthrough: 'Quick' suggests speed, but its archaic sense is living.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe a creature that is living rather than dead, the older sense surviving in the biblical phrase.

clue.text: Something worn by woman in part of France

blocks.note: first meaning: a skirt or dress reaching to mid-calf
second meaning: the south of the country

explanation.surface: What a woman wears in a region of France.
explanation.definitionFit: A midi is a calf-length skirt or coat, and the Midi is the French name for the southern region of the country.

clue.text: Pistol's turning up, in another Shakespeare role

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up means reading from the bottom to the top

blocks.note: read as pistols, plural: these are weapons

explanation.surface: Pistol, the Shakespeare swaggerer, turns up in a different part.
explanation.walkthrough: Pistol is himself a Shakespeare character, hence 'another'. Snug is the joiner who plays the Lion in A Midsummer Night's Dream.
explanation.definitionFit: Snug the joiner is one of the rude mechanicals in A Midsummer Night's Dream, a part in a Shakespeare play.

clue.text: Cloak what managers do

blocks.note: first meaning: a long ceremonial cape worn by priests
second meaning: to manage is to get by, deal with things

explanation.walkthrough: 'Managers' are not bosses: they are people who manage, that is who get by.
explanation.definitionFit: A cope is a priest's long vestment, and to cope is to handle difficulties successfully.

clue.text: Bishop's call for Church festival

blocks.note: first meaning: an official inspection visit by a bishop to the parishes of a diocese
second meaning: the feast marking Mary's visit to Elizabeth, kept on 2 July

explanation.surface: A bishop issues a summons to a church celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Call' means a visit, not a summons.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a formal pastoral visit by a prelate and also the feast day of the Virgin Mary's visit to her cousin.

clue.text: Rent one end of terrace

definitions.note: a past-tense verb here: rent is the past of rend

indicators.note: a word has two ends, and 'one end' leaves the choice open between the first letter and the last

blocks.note: the front end of terrace
one end or the other: the choice between the two ends is spelt out as the word or
the back end of terrace

explanation.surface: A landlord charges rent on the house at the end of a row of terraced houses.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is in the phrasing: one end of terrace is either its first letter or its last, so the answer is just that choice written out.
explanation.definitionFit: To rend is to tear apart violently, and its past tense matches the past tense of tear exactly.

clue.text: Basic conclusion of inquiry concealed by minion

indicators.note: the conclusion of a word is its final letter, the only one kept
something concealed by another thing is tucked away inside it

blocks.note: an underling is a minion, a subordinate
the final letter of inquiry

explanation.surface: The basic result of an investigation is hushed up by a junior official.
explanation.walkthrough: The last letter of inquiry goes inside UNDERLING, between its L and I.
explanation.definitionFit: Underlying means fundamental, lying beneath the surface as the root cause, just as basic does.
